title: Sprint 5 — Stripe, Webhooks, Idempotency & Integration Testing
summary: Replace the stub payment with Stripe Checkout, verify Webhook signatures, prevent duplicates, and test the entire flow.

briefBlocks.text: Sprint 5 — Stripe, Webhooks, Idempotency & Integration Testing

briefBlocks.markdown: **DonationHub** is a donation and charity campaign management platform. Until the end of Sprint 4, a donation was completed through a temporary stub endpoint (`mark-succeeded`) so you could build the success flow, receipts, and emails without a payment gateway. In this sprint, you replace that stub with a real payment gateway: **Stripe Checkout**, receive payment results via cryptographically signed **Webhooks**, protect the system against duplicate requests with **Idempotency**, and prove that the entire journey works through **integration tests** against a real SQL Server database.

This sprint deals with **money**: any mistake here means a donor gets charged twice, or a campaign is credited with funds that were never actually paid. Therefore, correctness and security come before speed.

- **Duration:** 15 Days (22/12/2026 to 05/01/2027)
- **Stand-up 1 (Day 5):** 26/12/2026 — Session Leader: **Asma ELhadidy**
- **Stand-up 2 (Day 10):** 31/12/2026 — Session Leader: **Kareem Zein**
- **Closing & Deadline (Day 15):** 05/01/2027 — Session Leader: **Mohamed Atef**
- **Code Review & Corrections (Days 16–18):** 06/01/2027 to 08/01/2027
- **Evaluation:** 100 Points

**Target Framework:** .NET 10 (`net10.0`) — fully compatible with .NET 8 and .NET 9. We continue with the same project decisions: `.slnx` solution, SQL Server with EF Core, **thin Controllers**, Clean Architecture with Vertical Slices, and MediatR `[12.5.0]`.

Replace the development payment stub with a production-ready payment gateway via **Stripe Checkout**. Safely process asynchronous payment notifications using **Stripe Webhooks** with cryptographic HMAC signature verification. Guarantee financial safety against network retries and duplicate webhooks via **API Idempotency** (the `Idempotency-Key` header and event deduplication). Validate complete, critical application workflows using real **Integration Tests** powered by `WebApplicationFactory` against a real SQL Server test database (**Testcontainers** is a BONUS option).

This is the flow you will build from clicking "Donate" to issuing the receipt:

briefBlocks.code:
Donor clicks Donate
        ↓
POST /donations/{id}/checkout
        ↓
Stripe Checkout Session Created (Minor Units / Cents)
        ↓
Donor Pays on Hosted Stripe Page
        ↓
Stripe Webhook (checkout.session.completed)
        ↓
Verify Stripe-Signature Header (EventUtility.ConstructEvent)
        ↓
Deduplicate Webhook Event (Idempotency Check)
        ↓
Verify Amount & Currency → Settle Donation (one transaction)
        ↓
Return 200 quickly → Enqueue Receipt PDF & Email After Commit (Hangfire)

briefBlocks.markdown: **Why not InMemory?** The EF Core InMemory provider does not support transactions, unique indexes, or `RowVersion` — which are precisely what you test in this sprint: preventing duplicate event insertion, preventing two donations with the same key, and safely updating `RaisedAmount` under concurrency. A test that passes on InMemory may fail on real SQL Server.
To receive Stripe webhooks on your local development machine:

items: Sign up for a free Stripe developer account and obtain **test mode** API keys only (`pk_test_...` and `sk_test_...`).
Store the secret key and webhook secret using `dotnet user-secrets` (or environment variables). **Never** put them in `appsettings*.json`.
If you cannot create a Stripe test account in your country, tell your mentor **before Stand-up 1 (26/12/2026)**.
Download and install the [Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/stripe-cli).
Authenticate via `stripe login`.
Forward webhooks to your local API: `stripe listen --forward-to https://localhost:7001/api/v1/payments/webhook`

The `appsettings.json` file in Git contains empty placeholders only. A secret key leaked into Git history is considered compromised even if you delete it in a later commit — revoke it from the Stripe Dashboard immediately.

briefBlocks.markdown:
These are four non-negotiable rules, and all payment code will be reviewed against them:

1. **Currency in Minor Units:** Stripe requires amounts in the smallest currency unit (e.g., USD cents: `$10.50` = `1050`). Never pass floating-point numbers directly; calculate integer minor units explicitly.
2. **Never Trust the Client:** The payment amount and associated campaign are determined by the **server** from the database, not client input. The Stripe Checkout session must lock the amount taken from the donation record in the database.
3. **"At-Least-Once" Delivery & Idempotency:** Stripe may redeliver the same webhook multiple times during network retries. Every event ID must be recorded and processed **exactly once**.
4. **The Webhook Is the Only Source of Truth:** A donation becomes `Succeeded` only from a verified webhook event, never from redirecting to the success URL — a client can open that URL without paying.

briefBlocks.code:
Amount in DB (decimal)      Stripe unit_amount (long)
$10.50                  →   1050
$25.00                  →   2500
$9,999.99               →   999999

✔  decimal.Round(amount * 100m, 0) → checked((long)...)
✘  (long)(10.50 * 100)  with double  → rounding surprises
✘  amount sent by the client in the checkout request

briefBlocks.markdown: **The success URL is not proof of payment.** The `SuccessUrl` page is purely a user experience page saying "Thank you". Anyone can type that URL into the browser. Never change any donation's status inside an endpoint serving the success URL — status changes happen **only** inside the webhook handler after signature verification.

Think of a webhook as a message that may arrive **twice or more, late, or out of order** (e.g., `checkout.session.expired` after `completed`). Design every handler so that executing it twice is equivalent to executing it once.
All tasks below are **CORE** unless marked **BONUS**.

| Task | Topic | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stripe Checkout session, payment status, and stub removal | PAY-01, PAY-02, PAY-03, PAY-09, PAY-10 |
| 2 | Webhook handler and signature verification | PAY-04, PAY-05, PAY-07, PAY-08 |
| 3 | Local webhook testing via Stripe CLI | PAY-10 + README |
| 4 | API and Webhook Idempotency | DON-10, §6.5, PAY-06 |
| 5 | Integration testing with WebApplicationFactory | §6.13 |

Implement the checkout initiation flow according to SRS §5.9. The donation is created beforehand in `Pending` status via `POST /campaigns/{campaignId}/donations` (from Sprint 3), and then its owner requests a payment session. The server reads the amount and campaign from the database, creates a Stripe Checkout session, persists a `PaymentAttempt` linked to it, and returns the URL of the Stripe-hosted payment page.

items: **PAY-01:** `POST /donations/{id}/checkout` (Owner only) creates a Stripe **Checkout Session** (`mode: payment`) for a `Pending` donation and returns the session's checkout URL.
**PAY-02:** The session carries `client_reference_id` = `donation.Id.ToString()`.
**PAY-02:** Metadata dictionary containing `donationId` and `campaignId`.
**PAY-02:** Single line item: Campaign Title as name, amount converted to **minor units** (cents), and currency from configuration.
**PAY-02:** Success and Cancel callback URLs defined in `StripeOptions`.
**PAY-03:** Create and persist a `PaymentAttempt` for each session: `DonationId`, `StripeCheckoutSessionId`, `StripePaymentIntentId?`, `Amount`, `Status`, `CreatedAt`, `UpdatedAt`, `FailureCode?`.
**PAY-03:** Status values: `Created`, `Succeeded`, `Failed`, `Expired`. A donor may start a new attempt for the same pending donation if a prior session was abandoned.
**Payment status:** `GET /donations/{id}/payment-status` (Owner and Admin) returns the donation status and its latest payment attempt status. Another user's donation returns **404**.

**PAY-10:** Stripe **test mode** keys only. `StripeOptions` (secret key, webhook secret, currency, success/cancel URLs) is validated with `ValidateOnStart()`, and secret values come from `dotnet user-secrets` or environment variables, never from `appsettings*.json`.
**PAY-09:** Remove the temporary stub endpoint `POST /admin/donations/{id}/mark-succeeded` (DON-06) and its handler. From now on, **only the webhook** can complete a donation.

briefBlocks.markdown:
**Endpoints in this task** (base path `/api/v1`):

| Method | Path | Access | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| POST | `/campaigns/{campaignId}/donations` | D, M, Adm | Create a `Pending` donation (exists from Sprint 3; now requires `Idempotency-Key`) |
| POST | `/donations/{id}/checkout` | Owner | Create a Checkout session and return the checkout URL |
| GET | `/donations/{id}/payment-status` | Owner, Adm | Donation status + latest `PaymentAttempt` status |
| ~~POST~~ | ~~`/admin/donations/{id}/mark-succeeded`~~ | — | **Removed in this sprint (PAY-09)** |

**Required Checkout session payload (PAY-02):**

| Stripe Field | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `payment` | Constant |
| `client_reference_id` | `donation.Id.ToString()` | Database |
| `metadata` | `donationId`, `campaignId` | Database |
| `line_items[0].price_data.product_data.name` | Campaign title | Database |
| `line_items[0].price_data.unit_amount` | Amount in minor units (`long`) | `donation.Amount` |
| `line_items[0].price_data.currency` | e.g., `usd` | `StripeOptions` |
| `line_items[0].quantity` | `1` | Constant |
| `success_url` / `cancel_url` | Frontend URLs | `StripeOptions` |
Example request and response (the exact response shape is your decision, but it must contain the checkout URL):

**Amount in minor units and from the server only:** The endpoint does not accept any amount in the body. The amount is read from `donation.Amount` in the database and converted to `long` in cents (`25.00` → `2500`) before sending to Stripe. Sending `25` instead of `2500` means the donor pays 25 cents!

**Multiple attempts for the same donation:** If the donor opens the payment page and then closes it, they can request `checkout` again; a new session and a new `PaymentAttempt` with status `Created` are created. The donation itself stays `Pending` until a successful webhook arrives. However, a donation in `Succeeded` or `Failed` status cannot start a new session (`Donation.InvalidState` — 409).

**PAY-09 — Removing the stub is not optional:** Delete the action, the command/handler, and the tests associated with `mark-succeeded`. Keep **the success flow logic itself** (DON-07: single transaction, `ReceiptNumber`, `RaisedAmount`, campaign completion) because the webhook will reuse it. The reviewer will search the codebase for any remaining trace of the endpoint.

git grep -n -i "mark-succeeded"

briefBlocks.text: Task 2 — Stripe Webhook Handling & Signature Verification

briefBlocks.markdown: Implement the secure webhook handler according to SRS §5.9. This endpoint is the **only place** where a donation transitions to `Succeeded`, so it must reject any request not signed by Stripe, verify the amount, and finish its work quickly.

items: **PAY-04:** Provide `POST /api/v1/payments/webhook` accepting the raw payload from Stripe. The endpoint is anonymous — the signature is the authentication — and is **excluded from rate limiting** (SRS §6.4).
**Cryptographic Verification:** Read the raw request body stream and the `Stripe-Signature` header, and verify the HMAC signature using the webhook secret (see code below).
If verification fails, return **400 Bad Request** immediately.

**PAY-05 — `checkout.session.completed`:** Extract `client_reference_id`, retrieve the donation and its payment attempt, and run the SRS §5.5 success flow in **one transaction**: donation `Succeeded` + `CompletedAt` + `ReceiptNumber`, attempt `Succeeded`, add the amount to `RaisedAmount`, and campaign `Completed` when the goal is reached.
**PAY-05:** A payment that arrives after the campaign has expired or completed is still accepted and logged as a warning.
**PAY-05 — `checkout.session.expired`:** Mark the attempt `Expired`.
**PAY-05 — `payment_intent.payment_failed`:** Mark the attempt `Failed` (storing `FailureCode`), and mark the donation `Failed` when no other attempt can still succeed.
**PAY-05:** Unknown sessions or unhandled event types are logged and answered with **200**.
**PAY-07 (Amount Verification):** Verify that the paid amount (minor units) and currency match the donation. A mismatch is logged as an **error** and does **not** complete the donation.
**PAY-08 (Fast Response):** The webhook returns 200 quickly. Heavy work (receipt PDF, emails) is **enqueued to Hangfire after the commit**, never executed inside the webhook request.

briefBlocks.markdown: Signature verification takes one line from the Stripe.net library:
If verification fails, the method throws `StripeException` — catch it and return **400 Bad Request** immediately, before any database read or write (error code `Payment.InvalidSignature`).

**Required events and what must happen:**

| Event | Action | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `checkout.session.completed` | Verify amount and currency → §5.5 success flow in one transaction → jobs after commit | 200 |
| `checkout.session.expired` | Attempt `Expired` | 200 |
| `payment_intent.payment_failed` | Attempt `Failed` + `FailureCode`; donation `Failed` if no open attempt remains | 200 |
| Unknown session / unhandled event | Log only | 200 |
| Duplicate event (same `event.id`) | Ignore (Task 4) | 200 |
| Invalid or missing signature | Nothing changes | **400** |
| Amount or currency mismatch | Log at error level, donation stays `Pending` | 200 |

**Never trust the redirect to the success URL; trust only the signed webhook.** The redirect happens in the user's browser and can be forged, or may not happen at all (e.g., the user closed the browser right after paying). The webhook comes directly from Stripe's servers and is signed with a secret known only to you and Stripe.

**Read the raw body as-is:** Do not use `[FromBody]` with a custom model and do not re-serialize JSON before verification; the signature is computed over the original bytes, and any change in whitespace or property order breaks it. Read `Request.Body` as a string and pass it verbatim to `ConstructEvent`. Also make sure no request-logging middleware consumes the body before you.

**Late Payment (SRS §5.5):** If `checkout.session.completed` arrives after the campaign has become `Expired` or `Completed`, the donor has already been charged. **Accept the payment**, mark the donation `Succeeded`, add the amount to `RaisedAmount` without changing the campaign status, and log a warning. Refunds are a BONUS task.

**PAY-07 — The amount in the event is not automatically trusted:** Compare `amount_total` and `currency` from the session against the amount calculated from `donation.Amount` and the configured currency. On any mismatch: log an **error** with a structured template containing both amounts, do not complete the donation, and return 200 (redelivering will not fix the data).

**PAY-08:** Stripe has a short response timeout and retries delivery if you take too long or return an error. Therefore, inside the request: verify → update state → `SaveChanges` → `Enqueue`, then return 200. Generating the PDF and sending the email happen in the Sprint 4 jobs (JOB-01 and JOB-02) after the commit — never before, so no receipt is sent for a donation whose transaction rolled back.

briefBlocks.text: Task 3 — Local Webhook Testing via Stripe CLI

briefBlocks.markdown: Stripe cannot reach `localhost` on your machine. The Stripe CLI solves this: it receives events from your test account and forwards them to your local API, signed with its own signing secret.

items: Run your application locally (e.g., on `https://localhost:7001`).
Execute `stripe listen --forward-to https://localhost:7001/api/v1/payments/webhook`.

Capture the temporary webhook signing secret displayed by the CLI (`whsec_...`) and store it via `dotnet user-secrets set "Stripe:WebhookSecret" "whsec_..."` (or an environment variable). **Never** put it in `appsettings.Development.json` or any file tracked in Git.
Trigger test events: `stripe trigger checkout.session.completed`, `stripe trigger checkout.session.expired`, and `stripe trigger payment_intent.payment_failed`, and confirm your API handles each one.
Document these steps in a README section titled **"How to test Stripe locally"**.

briefBlocks.code:
# 1) Run the API
dotnet run --project src/DonationHub.Api --launch-profile https

# 2) In a second terminal: forward events to the API
stripe listen --forward-to https://localhost:7001/api/v1/payments/webhook
#    > Ready! Your webhook signing secret is whsec_xxxxxxxx (^C to quit)

# 3) Store the displayed secret, then restart the API
dotnet user-secrets set "Stripe:WebhookSecret" "whsec_xxxxxxxx" --project src/DonationHub.Api

# 4) In a third terminal: trigger the events
stripe trigger checkout.session.completed
stripe trigger checkout.session.expired
stripe trigger payment_intent.payment_failed

briefBlocks.markdown:
| Command | What You Should See |
|---|---|
| `stripe trigger checkout.session.completed` | `200` in the `stripe listen` window, and a log saying the session is unknown (because the CLI generated it itself) |
| `stripe trigger checkout.session.expired` | `200`, and the payment attempt becomes `Expired` if the session is known |
| `stripe trigger payment_intent.payment_failed` | `200`, and a log with the event and failure code |
| Change the secret in user-secrets to a wrong value then trigger | `400` in the `stripe listen` window |

**`stripe trigger` creates its own test objects** unrelated to your donations, so the right behavior is a warning-level log and then 200. To genuinely test the full flow: create a donation, request `checkout`, open the `checkoutUrl`, pay with Stripe's test card `4242 4242 4242 4242` (any future expiry date and any CVC), and watch `payment-status` transition to `Succeeded`.

The `whsec_...` secret printed by `stripe listen` is specific to your machine and account; if it reaches Git, consider it compromised. Never put it in `appsettings.Development.json`, even if the file is "for development only".

The README must include a **How to test Stripe locally** section explaining: creating a test mode account, storing keys with user-secrets, running `stripe listen`, copying the `whsec`, the three `stripe trigger` commands, and testing a full payment with the test card. This section will be used during grading.

Implement idempotency safeguards according to SRS §6.5. Networks are unreliable: a mobile app might send the same "Donate" request twice because the response was delayed, and Stripe might send the same event twice. In both cases, the outcome must be **as if the request arrived only once**.
**First: API Request Idempotency (DON-10 / §6.5)**

items: `POST /campaigns/{campaignId}/donations` and `POST /donations/{id}/checkout` **require** the `Idempotency-Key` header. A missing key returns **400**.
Store each key in `IdempotencyRecord`: `Key`, `UserId`, `RequestHash`, `ResponseStatusCode`, `ResponseBody`, `CreatedAt`, `ExpiresAt`.
Same key + same user + same body: return the stored response **without repeating the action**.
Same key + different body: return **422** with error code `Idempotency.KeyReusedWithDifferentRequest`.
Keys expire after **24 hours**.
Two simultaneous requests with the same key must not create two donations (e.g., a unique index on `Key` + `UserId`, inserted **before** the action runs).

briefBlocks.markdown:
| Scenario | Response |
|---|---|
| First request with a new key | Action executes; response is stored (e.g., 201) |
| Repeating the same request with the same key and same body | Same status and same stored body, **without** a new donation |
| Same key with a different body (another amount) | **422** `Idempotency.KeyReusedWithDifferentRequest` |
| Missing `Idempotency-Key` header | **400** |
| Same key from **another user** | Treated as an independent key (the key is unique per user) |
| Same key after 24 hours have passed | Treated as a new request |

briefBlocks.code:
POST /api/v1/campaigns/9d1e.../donations
Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
Idempotency-Key: 6f1b0c1e-8a53-4c3a-9a9c-0d6f9d0c2f11
Content-Type: application/json

{ "amount": 25.00 }

→ 201 Created   { "id": "7a2c...", "status": "Pending", ... }

-- the same request again (client retry after a timeout) --
→ 201 Created   { "id": "7a2c...", "status": "Pending", ... }   (same body, no new row)

-- same key, different body: { "amount": 50.00 } --
→ 422 Unprocessable Entity   code: Idempotency.KeyReusedWithDifferentRequest

briefBlocks.markdown: **Concurrency is the real test:** The naive "check for key; if missing, execute then store" approach fails when two requests arrive at the exact same moment — neither finds the key, so both execute. The solution: **insert the record first** (in an "in progress" state) with a unique index on (`Key`, `UserId`), so the second insert fails at the database level; then execute the action and update the record with the response.

The `Idempotency-Key` is generated by the **client** (usually a UUID) once per user-intended operation, and reused on every retry of that same operation. Two intentional clicks on "Donate" = two different keys.
**Second: Webhook Event Deduplication (PAY-06)**

items: Store each processed Stripe event in a `ProcessedStripeEvent` record (`EventId` as primary key, `Type`, `ProcessedAt`), saved in **the same transaction** as the event's changes.
If an incoming event ID already exists, acknowledge receipt immediately with **HTTP 200 OK** and ignore the duplicate to prevent double-crediting campaign funds.

briefBlocks.markdown: **Why the same transaction?** If you saved `ProcessedStripeEvent` and then saving the donation failed, the event would be considered processed and the donation would never complete. Conversely, if you saved the donation and then saving the event record failed, a redelivery would credit the amount a second time. Saving both together in a single `SaveChanges` ensures they succeed together or fail together.

**Third: Error Format** — Errors follow the shared Error catalogue (`Code`, `Message`, `Type`) and are returned as ProblemDetails (RFC 9457) containing `code`, `traceId`, and `errors` for validation errors:

briefBlocks.code:
{
  "type": "https://httpstatuses.io/422",
  "title": "The Idempotency-Key was already used with a different request.",
  "status": 422,
  "code": "Idempotency.KeyReusedWithDifferentRequest",
  "traceId": "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01"
}

briefBlocks.text: Task 5 — Integration Testing with WebApplicationFactory (Testcontainers as BONUS)

briefBlocks.markdown: Create `DonationHub.Api.IntegrationTests` (SRS §6.13). Unit tests prove each component works in isolation; integration tests prove the components work **together**: routing, authentication, filters, EF Core, unique constraints, and transactions — through real HTTP requests to your application.

items: Configure `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` to bootstrap the API in-memory (in-memory test server).
Run the tests against a **real SQL Server test database** (a Docker Compose service or LocalDB). Never use the EF Core InMemory provider.
**BONUS:** Use **Testcontainers for .NET** to spin up a disposable SQL Server container for the test suite.
Never call real Stripe or real SMTP in tests: build webhook payloads locally and sign them with a test webhook secret, and replace the email sender with a fake.
`dotnet test` runs all tests without any additional manual step (other than having SQL Server running).

briefBlocks.markdown: **Forbidden in tests:** the EF Core InMemory provider, calling `api.stripe.com`, sending emails via a real SMTP server, and putting a real `sk_test` key in test code. The test suite must pass on the mentor's machine and in CI without internet access to Stripe.

**Minimum six required scenarios:**

| # | Scenario | Expected Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Register then login | 200/201 then a valid access token |
| 2 | Create campaign (Admin) then donation (Donor) | Donation `Pending` |
| 3 | Webhook success flow with a locally signed payload | Donation `Succeeded` and `RaisedAmount` updated |
| 4 | Duplicate webhook event | Funds credited once, second call returns 200 |
| 5 | Invalid signature | 400, and nothing changed in the database |
| 6 | Replay request with same `Idempotency-Key` | Same response, and no second donation |
**The critical user journey** that at least one end-to-end test must cover:

briefBlocks.code:
Register Donor
     ↓
Authenticate & Receive JWT
     ↓
Create Campaign as Admin
     ↓
Create Donation as Donor (Pending)
     ↓
Simulate Valid Stripe Webhook Delivery
     ↓
Assert Donation is Succeeded & Campaign RaisedAmount is Updated

briefBlocks.markdown: **How to sign a payload locally:** The `Stripe-Signature` header has the format `t={unix-timestamp},v1={signature}`, where `signature` = lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of `"{timestamp}.{payload}"` using the webhook secret as the key. Configure the same test secret (e.g., `whsec_integration_tests_secret`) in the factory's settings so the real `EventUtility.ConstructEvent` accepts it without mocking verification.

dotnet add tests/DonationHub.Api.IntegrationTests package Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing
dotnet add tests/DonationHub.Api.IntegrationTests package FluentAssertions --version 7.0.0

briefBlocks.title: 🔄 Integration Testing in ASP.NET Core — Julio Casal
briefBlocks.description: Alternative explanation of integration testing in ASP.NET Core using WebApplicationFactory and service replacement.

items: Stripe Checkout session generation endpoint returning a valid Stripe redirect URL (PAY-01 to PAY-03).
`GET /donations/{id}/payment-status` for the owner and Admin.
Cryptographically verified webhook endpoint using `EventUtility.ConstructEvent`, handling the three PAY-05 events with amount and currency verification (PAY-07).
Webhook event deduplication via `ProcessedStripeEvent` records (PAY-06).
`Idempotency-Key` handling with `IdempotencyRecord` on donation creation and checkout (DON-10, §6.5).
Removal of the `mark-succeeded` stub (PAY-09).
Local testing workflow documented in the README using Stripe CLI.
Integration test suite (`WebApplicationFactory` + real SQL Server test database) covering the six SRS §6.13 scenarios.
Creating a checkout session produces a valid URL and stores a `PaymentAttempt` with status `Created`.
Tampered or unsigned webhook requests are rejected with HTTP 400.
Sending the exact same webhook payload twice does not increment campaign funds a second time; the duplicate is answered with 200.
`checkout.session.expired` marks the attempt `Expired`, and `payment_intent.payment_failed` marks it `Failed`.
An amount or currency mismatch is logged as an error and does not complete the donation.
The donation becomes `Succeeded` only via the webhook, never via the success URL.
The webhook does no PDF or email work inline; these jobs are enqueued after the commit.
The temporary endpoint `POST /admin/donations/{id}/mark-succeeded` no longer exists.
Repeating a request with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the stored response without creating duplicate entities; a missing key returns 400, and a reused key with a different body returns 422.
`dotnet test` runs all integration tests against a real SQL Server test database, without calling real Stripe or SMTP.
The README is updated for this sprint, including the **how to test Stripe locally** section.
No secrets (Stripe keys, webhook secret) exist in the repository history.
The `sprint-5` tag exists and points to the final commit.

briefBlocks.markdown: Optional — counts only after **all** CORE items pass.

items: **PAY-11:** Admin refund of a succeeded donation (see DON-13).
**PAY-12:** Handle the `charge.refunded` webhook event.
**DON-13:** Refund of a succeeded donation (Admin), with the amount subtracted from the campaign's `RaisedAmount`.
**Testcontainers:** Run the integration tests against a disposable SQL Server container.
**IDN-13:** Refresh token reuse detection (if not done in an earlier sprint): using an already-revoked token revokes the whole token family.

briefBlocks.title: Building Resilient Cloud Microservices with Polly (.NET Foundation)
briefBlocks.description: Building resilient services against network failures with Polly: retries, circuit breaker, and timeouts — useful when calling external payment gateways.

solutionBlocks.markdown: This is a reference solution that illustrates a sound **way of thinking** for each task, not the only approach. It builds on the same codebase from the previous sprints. Focus on the **why** behind each decision: in this sprint you will often be asked "What happens if the request arrives twice?" and "What if saving fails midway?".

To keep things concise, repetitive parts (validators, DTOs, and some registrations) have been omitted, while the important parts are written out in full. Shared names follow the Sprint 2–4 definitions: `Result`/`Result<T>` in `DonationHub.Domain.Common` with implicit conversions from `Error` and from value, `ApiControllerBase.ProblemFrom(error)`, `IReceiptNumberGenerator`, `IEmailService`, and `IBackgroundJobScheduler` — if your names differ, match yours accordingly.

solutionBlocks.text: Task 1 — Checkout Session, PaymentAttempt, and Stub Removal

solutionBlocks.markdown:
**Why is `PaymentAttempt` separate from `Donation`?** A donation is the "intent to donate an amount to a campaign", whereas an attempt is "a single payment session on Stripe". A donor may open multiple sessions for the same donation, and each session has an independent lifecycle. Separating them lets us track each session and link any webhook event to it via `StripeCheckoutSessionId` without polluting the donation state.

We generate the attempt ID **before** calling Stripe so we can include it in the metadata; that way, the `payment_intent.payment_failed` event (which does not include session data) tells us which attempt failed.
**Minor units** are calculated in one place only, using `decimal` and `checked` so any overflow surfaces as an error instead of silently producing a wrong number:

Never write `(long)(amount * 100)` with `double`: `0.29 * 100` in `double` equals `28.999999999999996`, and casting truncates it to `28`. The same reasoning makes `decimal` the right type for money in entities and in EF (`HasPrecision(18, 2)`).

**Abstraction in Application:** The `Application` layer has no knowledge of Stripe.net. We intentionally define two separate contracts: `IPaymentGateway` (calls the Stripe network API to create a session) and `IPaymentWebhookVerifier` (completely local: HMAC and JSON parsing). This separation lets integration tests replace the gateway with a fake while keeping signature verification **real**.

**`StripeOptions`** follows the Sprint 1 pattern: `BindConfiguration` + `ValidateDataAnnotations` + `ValidateOnStart`. The constraints here are not cosmetic; the regex on `sk_test_` literally enforces PAY-10 — the application **refuses to start** with a live key:

**The handler:** We verify ownership (404 rather than 403 — SRS §6.3), verify that the donation is `Pending` and the campaign still accepts donations, then call Stripe, and then save the attempt. The "Stripe first, then DB" ordering is intentional: we need `session.Id` to persist the attempt, and if saving fails after creating the session, the donor will never see its URL and the session will simply expire on its own (an `expired` event for an unknown session is logged and answered with 200).

**Session timeout vs. DON-09:** The Sprint 4 job fails a pending donation after 30 minutes, whereas a Stripe session can remain open for 60 minutes. If a donor pays at minute 40, a payment will arrive for a `Failed` donation. Have the job check first: if there is a `Created` attempt whose session has not expired yet, reschedule itself for after `ExpiresAt` instead of failing the donation. And when creating a new session, you can (optionally) expire prior open sessions with `SessionService.ExpireAsync` so the same donation cannot be paid twice.

**Payment status** is read-only, so it goes through `IReadDbContext` (`Donations` has been in it since Sprint 3; add `PaymentAttempts` without tracking). The projection returns the enums themselves, and `JsonStringEnumConverter` configured since Sprint 2 serializes them as strings:

**PAY-09 — Removing the stub:** We delete the endpoint, the command, and its tests, while **keeping** the success flow logic: `Donation.MarkSucceeded`, `IReceiptNumberGenerator`, and the single-transaction rules are all reused by the webhook. If the success logic was inside the stub handler itself, move it to a shared place first, then delete the stub.

solutionBlocks.text: Task 2 — The Webhook: Signature, Events, and Single Transaction

solutionBlocks.markdown: **Core idea:** The controller knows nothing about Stripe; it reads the raw text and header and passes them to a command. The handler asks `IPaymentWebhookVerifier` to verify and map to `PaymentWebhookEvent`, then deduplicates, dispatches by event type, saves **everything in one `SaveChanges`** (the state changes + the event record), and only after the commit succeeds does it enqueue the jobs.

`[DisableRateLimiting]` bypasses the global limiter for this endpoint as well. If you applied a rate-limit policy via `RequireRateLimiting` across all controllers, make sure this attribute overrides it. And if you have a `FallbackPolicy` requiring authentication, `[AllowAnonymous]` is mandatory — otherwise Stripe will receive 401 and keep retrying endlessly.

**The Verifier** is the only place aware of Stripe.net in the webhook flow. It catches `StripeException` (invalid signature, or a timestamp older than 5 minutes — protecting against replay attacks) and maps it to `PaymentErrors.InvalidSignature` (`new Error("Payment.InvalidSignature", ..., ErrorType.Validation)` → 400):

**Stripe.net:** `throwOnApiVersionMismatch: false` prevents rejecting an event whose `api_version` (from your account, the CLI, or test payloads) differs from the library version; the cleaner alternative is pinning the webhook endpoint's API version in the Stripe Dashboard. `EventTypes` constants are `const string`, so they work in switch expressions.

**Specialized repository:** `ProcessedStripeEvent` is not an `Entity` (its key is string `EventId`), and some queries are payment-specific, so we define `IPaymentsRepository`. What matters is that it uses the **same** scoped `AppDbContext` used by `IUnitOfWork`, so everything it adds participates in the same `SaveChanges` — i.e., the same transaction:

**Webhook handler — overall structure:** Verification → deduplication → dispatch → single save → jobs. Notice the race-condition handling: if the same event arrives in two concurrent requests, both pass the "already processed?" check, but the primary key on `EventId` causes the second save to fail; we catch the error, confirm it is indeed a duplicate, and return 200.

**`checkout.session.completed`:** We correlate the event to the attempt via the session ID, verify that `client_reference_id` matches the attempt's donation, verify PAY-07 against **database** values, and then execute DON-07 using the same Sprint 3 building blocks: `Donation.MarkSucceeded` (amount + campaign completion) and `IReceiptNumberGenerator`. **Why not call `DonationSuccessFlow` directly?** Because it owns its own `SaveChanges`, and on a `RowVersion` conflict it calls `ClearChangeTracker()`, wiping out the attempt update and the `ProcessedStripeEvent` record — which breaks PAY-06 (same transaction). So the handler preserves its exact guarantees: late-payment warning, retrying on `RowVersion`, and jobs and cache invalidation after commit:

**A mismatch is logged, yet the event is marked as processed.** This is intentional: redelivering the same event will not change the amount, so returning 500 and making Stripe retry for days serves no purpose. The error-level log is the alert for humans. However, **never complete the donation** in this case.

**`expired` and `payment_failed`:** Both are inherently idempotent — if the attempt is not `Created`, we do nothing (events can arrive out of order). The donation is marked failed only when no other open attempt remains:

**A trade-off you should be ready to explain:** The Checkout page allows the donor to try another card **within the same session** after the first one is declined. The requirement states "the donation becomes `Failed` when no other attempt can still succeed", so we applied it literally to other attempts. The rare edge case: a donation becomes `Failed` and then `completed` arrives for that same session — we record the attempt as `Succeeded` and log an error for manual refund (DON-13 BONUS).

**Between commit and Enqueue there is a small gap:** If the process crashes after saving and before `Enqueue`, the donation completes without a receipt. This is acceptable within the project scope, and is solved either by a recurring job checking for "Succeeded donations without a `ReceiptFileName`", or via the Transactional Outbox pattern (storing the message in the same transaction). Mention this as a conscious decision in your README.

**Concurrency on the campaign (DON-08):** Two successful events for two different donations to the same campaign may conflict on `RowVersion`. The loop in `Handle` mirrors `DonationSuccessFlow`: on `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`, nothing was saved (not even the event record), so we clear the change tracker and re-apply the update against fresh data up to 3 times using the same receipt number; if the conflict persists, we return 500 so Stripe retries later as a last line of defense. As for `ProcessedStripeEvent`, it is a simple entity (`EventId` primary key, `Type`, `ProcessedAt`) with a `Create` method.

solutionBlocks.text: Task 3 — Stripe CLI and the README Section

solutionBlocks.markdown: There is no code here, but documentation is part of the evaluation. A good section lets a mentor who has never seen your project test payments in 5 minutes. Notice that commands are indented inside the README:

solutionBlocks.code:
## How to test Stripe locally

1. Create a free Stripe account and stay in **test mode** (keys start with `sk_test_`).
2. Store the secrets with user-secrets (never in `appsettings*.json`):

        cd src/DonationHub.Api
        dotnet user-secrets set "Stripe:SecretKey" "sk_test_..."

3. Run the API on `https://localhost:7001`, then forward webhooks:

        stripe login
        stripe listen --forward-to https://localhost:7001/api/v1/payments/webhook

4. Copy the `whsec_...` secret printed by `stripe listen` and restart the API:

        dotnet user-secrets set "Stripe:WebhookSecret" "whsec_..."

5. Trigger the three handled events (they create their own objects, so the API logs
   "unknown session" and answers 200):

        stripe trigger checkout.session.completed
        stripe trigger checkout.session.expired
        stripe trigger payment_intent.payment_failed

6. Full flow: `POST /api/v1/campaigns/{id}/donations` (with `Idempotency-Key`), then
   `POST /api/v1/donations/{id}/checkout`, open `checkoutUrl`, pay with card
   `4242 4242 4242 4242`, and check `GET /api/v1/donations/{id}/payment-status`.

solutionBlocks.text: Task 4 — Idempotency: API Filter and Event Log

solutionBlocks.markdown:
**Why an Action Filter instead of a MediatR Pipeline Behavior as in the video?** The requirement is to return **the exact same HTTP response** (status 201 and the body) — and that is an API-layer concept, not an Application-layer concept. The filter directly sees the header, the user, and the final `ObjectResult`, and is applied via an attribute on only the two endpoints. Moreover, the filter runs **after** authentication (so the user is known) and **after** `[ApiController]` automatic model validation.

**The hash** is computed over `ActionArguments` after binding (along with the route), so it includes both the body and the route ID, and is unaffected by whitespace or JSON property ordering.

**The store in Infrastructure:** The insert is committed immediately **before** running the action. A second concurrent request hits the primary key (SQL Server errors 2627 or 2601), reads the existing record, and decides: replay, mismatch, or in-progress. We detach the entity from the change tracker because `AppDbContext` is shared with the handler — otherwise the next `SaveChanges` would attempt to insert it again:

**The filter in Api:** It rejects a missing key with 400, returns the stored response verbatim, and stores any response below 500 (e.g., a 422 error is also replayed verbatim). On an exception or 500, we release the key so the client can actually retry. Applying it to the two endpoints is simply adding `[Idempotent]` alongside `[EnableRateLimiting(RateLimitPolicies.Donations)]` on the donation creation action (Sprint 3) and on `Checkout`:

**Our addition that you must be ready to defend:** Neither the SRS nor the brief specifies the response for a second request with the same key while the first is still running; we chose **409** with a new code `Idempotency.RequestInProgress` (not in the SRS catalogue, and this is how Stripe itself handles it), and the mandatory rule — no second donation — is satisfied in both cases. The alternative — waiting for the first request — complicates the code and ties up threads. Keep in mind that a replay does not return the `Location` header (it is not stored in `IdempotencyRecord`); if you want it, store important headers as well.

Cleanup: Expired records are deleted on demand inside `TryBeginAsync`, but add a simple recurring job so the table does not grow unbounded: `RecurringJob.AddOrUpdate<IdempotencyCleanupJob>("idempotency-cleanup", j => j.RunAsync(CancellationToken.None), Cron.Hourly);` and inside it run `ExecuteDeleteAsync` where `ExpiresAt <= now`.
**The Webhook (PAY-06)** is already covered in Task 2: a fast pre-check + primary key on `EventId` as the final guarantee + saving in the same `SaveChanges`.

**Strategy:** A single shared factory for all tests (`ICollectionFixture`) recreates the test database once at the start, and each test creates its own isolated data (unique email, new campaign) so tests never interfere with each other. We replace only four things: the gateway (no Stripe network calls), the email sender, the job scheduler (to assert what was enqueued), and `IDistributedCache` with an in-memory implementation instead of Redis. Every option with `ValidateOnStart` is configured via `UseSetting` because `Testing` does not load user-secrets or the Development settings file. **Signature verification stays real** — which is precisely what we want to test.

solutionBlocks.markdown: The `Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk` and `xunit.runner.visualstudio` versions are examples (use the latest stable version); the fixed requirements are FluentAssertions `[7.0.0]` (the last free-licensed version) and Moq `[4.18.4]` if you need it. The code targets xUnit v2; in v3, `IAsyncLifetime` returns `ValueTask` instead of `Task`.

**Checkpoints in your project:** (1) In .NET 10, the generated `Program` class is automatically public; in .NET 8/9, add `public partial class Program;` at the end of `Program.cs`. (2) If `Program.cs` reads a setting before `UseSetting` values take effect, use environment variables (`ConnectionStrings__Default`). (3) The `AppDbContext(DbContextOptions<AppDbContext>)` constructor must be accessible. (4) Raise the `auth` policy limits in the `Testing` environment, otherwise tests will hit 429.
**Signing a payload locally:** The exact algorithm Stripe uses — HMAC-SHA256 over `"{t}.{payload}"` using the full webhook secret as the key — so the real `EventUtility.ConstructEvent` accepts it:

**Hangfire in tests:** `AddHangfireServer` polls the test database and runs recurring jobs (such as JOB-04) that might mutate data during test execution; register it only outside the `Testing` environment (`if (!builder.Environment.IsEnvironment("Testing"))`).

items: Marking the donation `Succeeded` in the success URL endpoint or right after creating the session, instead of waiting for the webhook.
Receiving the webhook with `[FromBody] Event` or a custom model — signature verification becomes impossible or runs against re-serialized text.
Catching a signature failure and returning 200 "so Stripe doesn't retry" — 400 is required, and nothing must change.
Sending the amount to Stripe in dollars (`25`) instead of cents (`2500`), or calculating with `double`.
Failing to verify `amount_total` and `currency` in `checkout.session.completed` (PAY-07).
Saving `ProcessedStripeEvent` in a separate `SaveChanges` from the donation changes.
Generating PDFs or sending emails inside the webhook request, or enqueuing the job **before** the commit.
Implementing idempotency as "check, execute, then store" without a unique index inserted before execution — fails under concurrent requests.
Leaving the `mark-succeeded` endpoint or any code calling it.
Integration tests using EF Core InMemory, calling real Stripe, or requiring a real `sk_test` key to pass.
`whsec_...` or `sk_test_...` in `appsettings.Development.json` or in any previous commit.

solutionBlocks.text: Questions to Prepare for in Code Review

items: Why don't we trust the success URL? What happens if the donor closes the browser right after paying and before the redirect?
What exactly does HMAC protect? And why does the signature contain a timestamp? (Think about replay attacks and tolerance)
The exact same event arrives twice in the same millisecond: explain step by step why the amount is not credited twice in your code.
Why is `ProcessedStripeEvent` saved in the same transaction? What happens under each alternative ordering if the server crashes midway?
Two concurrent create-donation requests arrive with the same `Idempotency-Key`: where exactly does the second one fail? And what does the client see?
Why return 422 when reusing a key with a different body rather than 409? And why is the key scoped per user?
Why do we return 200 on an amount mismatch instead of 500? And when do we actually want Stripe to retry?
A payment arrives for an expired campaign: why do we accept it? And what is the risk if we reject it?
What do integration tests verify that unit tests cannot? And why not use InMemory?
What happens if the server crashes after the commit and before calling `Enqueue` for the receipt? And how do you handle it (Outbox)?

solutionBlocks.markdown: **DON-13 / PAY-11 (Admin Refund):** Add `RefundAsync(paymentIntentId, idempotencyKey)` to `IPaymentGateway` calling `RefundService`, then in the domain add `Donation.MarkRefunded(campaign, utcNow)` to subtract the amount from `RaisedAmount` and transition the status to `Refunded` (the bonus enum value). Decide and document: should a `Completed` campaign return to `Active` if the raised amount drops below the goal? (Invariant 8 says a final state cannot change.)

**PAY-12 (`charge.refunded`):** Add a case in the verifier for `EventTypes.ChargeRefunded` where `Data.Object` is a `Charge` (use `charge.PaymentIntentId` and `charge.AmountRefunded`), then correlate it to the attempt via `StripePaymentIntentId`. Make processing idempotent with Admin-initiated refunds: whichever arrives first transitions the state, and the second sees the donation is already `Refunded` and does not subtract the amount a second time.

**Testcontainers:** Replace the static connection string with a container started in `InitializeAsync` (package `Testcontainers.MsSql`). Build the container with `new MsSqlBuilder().WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest").Build()`, run `await _sql.StartAsync()` in `InitializeAsync`, then store `_sql.GetConnectionString()` and apply migrations to it, and dispose the container in `DisposeAsync`. Since `ConfigureWebHost` runs after `InitializeAsync`, the connection string is ready.

**IDN-13 (Refresh Token Reuse Detection):** Same hint as Sprint 1 — a **revoked** (not expired) token arriving again indicates potential theft: trace the `ReplacedByTokenId` chain and revoke all active tokens in the family, then return `Auth.RefreshTokenInvalid` (401). Add an integration test for it: refresh twice with the same token → the second gets 401, and the new token generated by the first refresh is also revoked.

If your solution satisfies the same **principles** — the signed webhook is the single source of truth, amounts are in minor units and server-derived, every event is processed once in a single transaction, duplicate requests never create duplicate entities even under concurrency, and tests prove all of this against real SQL Server — then you have built a payment system you can trust, even if the details differ.
